newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia seeks $1.45 billion in aid for 1997-99.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia seeks $1.45 billion in aid for 1997-99.

text.p: Cambodian officials on Monday told wary donors they sought $1.45 billion in international aid for the 1997-1999 period and said the country should not be penalised for its political woes or slow progress on reform.

The officials, speaking at a meeting with diplomats and aid representatives, were keen to put Cambodia in a positive light ahead of a July 1-2 gathering in Paris of a Consultative Group of donors to determine this year's aid level.
The Consultative Group, which comprises various lending agencies and countries such as Japan, will make commitments at its Paris meeting for mainly this year.
Cambodia has sought $449 million for calender 1997. The Consultative Group pledged $500 million last year.

Diplomats and donors at the meeting on Monday expressed some frustration with the lack of progress on illegal logging, the demobilisation of soldiers, trimming of the civil service, tax reform and that of the health and education sectors.
"The rhetoric and the reality are poles apart," one international donor consultant told reporters at the end of the meeting.
But Finance Minister Keat Chhon said Cambodia should not be faulted for its political woes or sometimes lacklustre reform efforts.
"Let me urge everyone interested in and actively assisting Cambodia to give us time and space to grow in the democratic process," he said.
"Judge us not harshly by such isolated and regrettable incidents," he said, adding that an average of $483 million per year in aid was key to the impoverished country's development.

Keat Chhon said despite a deadly March 30 grenade attack and recent bitter political feuds within the troubled coalition government, Cambodia's leaders remained "committed to democracy" and national elections in 1998.
Diplomats have said they want an end to infighting between co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen, who formed an uneasy coalition following U.N.-sponsored polls in 1993.
Keat Chhon and other officials tried to play down any concern that could jeopardise the nation's aid programme, which accounts for nearly half of the annual budget.

Sok An, co-Minister of the Council of Ministers, vowed to cut 7,300 more civil servants from government payrolls by the end of the year after cutting 7,669 between January and April. The government also pledged to demobilise 1,500 soldiers soon from the 145,000-strong military.

Minister of Agriculture Tao Seng Huor said Cambodia was making some progress in forestry policy reform, although he acknowledged there was room for improvement. He said illegal logging was on the decline.
The International Monetary Fund has warned that Cambodia must improve policing of its forests and accounting for revenues if it wants $40 million in loans.
